raw_case_text:
A 63-year-old white woman diagnosed with diabetes mellitus underwent right lung transplant for bronchiolitis obliterans syndrome (BOS) three years after an original left single lung transplant for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. Induction immunotherapy prior to re-transplantation consisted of antithymocyte globulin (ATG) and methylprednisolone. She had also received a course of ATG for management of BOS in her initial left lung transplant. Current maintenance immunosuppression included mycophenolate mofetil, tacrolimus, and prednisone, in addition to post-transplant antimicrobial prophylaxis with TMP-SMZ, valganciclovir, and itraconazole. She had multiple episodes of Epstein-Barr viremia within the first six months after transplant. She also experienced multiple infectious complications, including pseudomonas pneumonia, enterococcal tracheobronchitis, and most recently invasive right lower lobe pulmonary aspergillosis treated with isavuconazonium sulfate two and a half years after her redo lung transplant.
She presented to the emergency department three years after her redo lung transplant experiencing fluctuating, insidious-onset right lower abdominal pain. Her symptoms had been present for ten days and were associated with nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. Four weeks earlier, she had been prescribed oral antibiotics for a lower urinary tract infection. Upon presentation, the patient was afebrile with sinus tachycardia (heart rate: 114 beats per minute) and otherwise normal vital signs. Her chest and abdominal examinations were unremarkable. Her laboratory data were significant for mild neutrophilic leukocytosis of 14.6 x 106/microL, stable microcytic hypochromic anemia of 10.4 g/dl, and stable hyponatremia of 131 mmol/L. Urinalysis showed hazy urine with few squamous cells, >50 WBC, 3-10 RBCs, 30 mg/dl protein, moderate leukocyte esterase, and 11-25 hyaline casts/LPF.
An abdominal ultrasound revealed a 3.3 x 2.8 x 3.1 cm complex, solid-appearing mass within the mid-pole of the right kidney with peripheral vascularity. This mass was not seen on an abdominal computed tomogram (CT) performed four weeks earlier. A CT with contrast confirmed the 4.5 x 3.3 cm heterogeneous, enhancing soft tissue right renal mass with patent renal vein and no retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy (Figure 1). These imaging findings raised suspicion for renal cell carcinoma (RCC) and prompted magnetic resonance imaging of the abdomen. This showed a T1/T2 hypointense, diffusion-restricting, right mid-renal mass very suspicious for RCC. The patient subsequently underwent a staging positron emission tomography-CT that showed an intensely fluorodeoxyglucose-avid right renal mass (standard uptake value = 14.3) (Figure 2).
The patient was then evaluated by urology and oncology and underwent a hand-assisted right nephrectomy for a presumptive pre-operative diagnosis of RCC. Histopathology revealed a blue-green necrotic renal mass measuring 5.5 x 5 x 4 cm, located in the superior lateral pole, and compressing the superior calyx without pelvicalyceal involvement. There was no evidence of malignancy, but multiple filamentous bacteria consistent with the Nocardia species were identified. Methenamine silver stain showed filamentous bacteria-like structures staining positive on gram stain which were weakly positive on the Fite staining method, supporting a diagnosis of Nocardia renal abscess (Figure 3). CTs of the head and chest revealed no lesions suspicious for nocardiosis. Because the suspicion of RCC was extremely high based on imaging, the entire renal specimen was sent for pathological analysis as a fixed specimen but not for culture. Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) for Nocardia species on this nephrectomy specimen revealed N. paucivorans. She was subsequently started on dual therapy with imipenem and double strength TMP-SMZ. Imipenem was continued for 8 weeks, and TMP-SMZ was to be continued for 9 to 12 months thereafter.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 63-year-old white female bilateral sequential lung transplant recipient presented 3 years after her redo right lung transplant with a 10-day history of insidious, fluctuating right lower quadrant abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Ten days prior to presentation, the patient developed fluctuating right lower abdominal pain accompanied by nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. Four weeks earlier, she had been treated with oral antibiotics for a lower urinary tract infection and had a normal abdominal CT at that time.
subjective.past_medical_history: Diabetes mellitus; initial left single-lung transplant for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis complicated by bronchiolitis obliterans syndrome (treated with ATG), followed 3 years later (3 years prior to current presentation) by a redo right single-lung transplant with ATG and methylprednisolone induction, maintained on mycophenolate mofetil, tacrolimus, and prednisone alongside prophylactic TMP-SMZ, valganciclovir, and itraconazole. Post-transplant history included recurrent EBV viremia, Pseudomonas pneumonia, enterococcal tracheobronchitis, and invasive right lower lobe pulmonary aspergillosis treated with isavuconazonium sulfate 6 months prior.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea; afebrile. Home medications included mycophenolate mofetil, tacrolimus, prednisone, prophylactic TMP-SMZ, valganciclovir, and itraconazole.

objective.physical_examination: Afebrile with sinus tachycardia (heart rate 114 bpm) and otherwise normal vital signs; chest and abdominal examinations were unremarkable.
objective.routine_investigations: Labs showed mild neutrophilic leukocytosis (WBC 14.6 x 10^3/uL), stable microcytic hypochromic anemia (Hb 10.4 g/dL), and stable hyponatremia (131 mmol/L). Urinalysis showed hazy urine with few squamous cells, >50 WBC/HPF, 3-10 RBCs/HPF, 30 mg/dL protein, moderate leukocyte esterase, and 11-25 hyaline casts/LPF. Abdominal ultrasound revealed a new 3.3 x 2.8 x 3.1 cm complex solid-appearing mass in the mid-pole of the right kidney with peripheral vascularity.
objective.advanced_workup: Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT confirmed a 4.5 x 3.3 cm heterogeneous enhancing right renal soft-tissue mass with a patent renal vein and no retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy. Abdominal MRI showed a T1/T2-hypointense, diffusion-restricting right mid-renal mass, and staging 18F-FDG PET-CT demonstrated intense FDG avidity (SUV 14.3) suspicious for renal cell carcinoma. Head and chest CT scans showed no lesions suspicious for nocardiosis. Hand-assisted right radical nephrectomy was performed; gross and histopathological examination revealed a 5.5 x 5 x 4 cm blue-green necrotic abscess in the superior lateral pole without malignancy, containing Gram-positive, methenamine silver-positive, weakly Fite-positive filamentous branching bacteria.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Primary isolated right renal nocardiosis abscess caused by Nocardia paucivorans (masquerading radiologically as FDG-avid renal cell carcinoma despite TMP-SMZ prophylaxis) in a redo lung transplant recipient was confirmed via histopathology (Gram, methenamine silver, and Fite stains) and Nocardia species-specific PCR on the fixed nephrectomy specimen identifying Nocardia paucivorans. Following hand-assisted right nephrectomy, she was treated with intravenous imipenem for 8 weeks combined with oral double-strength trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMZ) planned for 9-12 months.
